item.title: Artificial Intelligence, Business, and Epochal Change
item.content:encoded:
Glen Whelan, ESG UQÀM

Gabriel Weber, ESSCA School of Management

Yann Truong, ESSCA School of Management

Ongoing developments in Artificial Intelligence (AI) indicate that machine learning technologies will not simply match, but will potentially significantly surpass, a wide range of human cognitive abilities. Given this trend, there is reason to believe that AI could threaten humanity's hegemonic, agentic, positioning and that it could be a driver of civilizational, epochal change.

Business actors occupy a unique dual-position within this context. First, as leading architects of AI development, high-tech corporations are rebuilding the organizational structures, labour markets, and human-machinic assemblages that will define social existence for decades to come by impacting upon such fundamental concerns as democracy, peace, and human flourishing. Second, the institution of business and markets as a whole will also find itself the subject of transformative forces that it cannot control despite the fact that certain actors therewithin – such as high-tech corporations – have given rise to them.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Speed versus safety in the rush to develop (super-intelligent) AI
  • Competition and conflict over AI resources
  • Defense, offense, and critical AI infrastructure
  • (Rogue) AI and principal-agent misalignment
  • AI and 'responsibility gaps'
  • Existential threats and AI
  • AI and the implicit/explicit embodiment of political goals and values
  • Corporate elites (e.g., owners/founders) and the control of AI
  • Corporate governance within the AI political context
  • Ideological conflict in the era of AI
  • The algocratic and epistocratic underpinnings of AI developments
  • AI and planetary boundaries
  • Environmental justice and AI
  • The global south and the AI workforce
  • Resource creation, extraction and commodification in the era of AI
  • AI and exosomatic energy use
  • AI and the changing value of human labour and human leisure
  • The possibility of human excellence and flourishing in AI impacted societies
  • AI and the transformation of markets for consumption and production
  • The implications of AI for how we conceive and value human rights, democracy and justice
  • AI and peace

item.title: Theoretical Contributions to Advance the Business and Society Debate
item.content:encoded:
Jay Joseph, American University of Beirut

Harry Van Buren III, University of Tennessee at Chattanooga

Jennifer Oetzel, American University

Angelika Rettberg, Universidad de los Andes

Global peace is needed now more than ever, yet "peace" still fails to feature in mainstream business and society debates. For over 20 years, "business and peace" has led this debate in business and management studies. Business and peace has generated a broad array of research studies that link business activity to peacebuilding; however, the high volume of descriptive, case-based, and practice-based research in the field, combined with the growing number of parallel contributions to conflict and peace-related topics in general management studies, presents challenges for moving a coherent debate on peace and business forward.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Stakeholder-based theories associated with business and peace
  • Systems perspectives on business and peace
  • Intergroup and contact theories in business contexts
  • Business and human rights frameworks
  • Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) and political CSR
  • Governance processes in business and peace
  • Organizing processes and organization studies
  • Normative and ethical frameworks addressing corruption and corporate misconduct
  • International business frameworks in conflict settings
  • Entrepreneurship and entrepreneurial models for conflict-resolution and peace
  • Advanced conceptual development for conflict and peace research
  • Boundary work to clarify field domains in business and peace
  • Theoretical consolidation and advancement of business and peace foundations

item.title: Collective actorhood and organizationality: Recalibrating responsibility in business-society relations
item.content:encoded:
Dennis Schoeneborn, Copenhagen Business School

Héloïse Berkowitz, CNRS, Aix Marseille University

Leonhard Dobusch, University of Innsbruck

Frank de Bakker, IÉSEG School of Management

Consuelo Vásquez, Université du Québec à Montréal (UQAM)

Over the past decades, the relations between business and society have fundamentally changed. We are entering an age of digital futures with artificial intelligence taking over more and more human tasks at rapid speed, as well as broken futures with accelerating dynamics of climate change, in which the survival of humankind will depend on our ability to organize in collective ways and imagine alternatives to tackle such complex social problems, amidst growing inequalities and ecological destruction on a planetary scale.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • How is collective actorhood performed and organized?
  • Is a legal status/legal person needed to accomplish collective actorhood?
  • Why and how do actors strategically downplay or amplify collective actorhood? How do these strategic efforts affect responsibility attributions?
  • What are the implications and limitations of collective actorhood for reenvisioning the business-society relationship and offer alternative solutions in crises of civilization?
  • Where and how does actorhood emerge? How do institutional contexts affect actorhood?
  • How does actorhood evolve over time or space, and how do organizations transition between different degrees of organizationality?
  • Can social collectives be perpetuated and maintained even with a low degree of organizationality – or do they feel pressures either to be dissolved or evolve toward higher degrees of organizationality eventually?
  • How to explain asymmetric dynamics between the organized (e.g., established formal organizations; high degree of organizationality) and the (rather) unorganized as their counterparts (e.g., social media firestorm; low degree of organizationality)?
  • What can we learn from alternative forms of organizing, including those in marginalized settings?
  • How is collective actorhood conceptualized in the various geographies, including the Global South? How does this translate, circulate, and adapt across geographies?
  • What are the contributions of other collective notions stemming from indigenous cosmovisions and decolonial approaches?
  • How does actorhood affect the interactions between organizations from different domains (for profit and non-profit, scientific organizations, public actors, etc.)?
  • When does collective actorhood create relations of domination and exploitation?
  • At what point does collective actorhood become constitutive of societal problems and crises (incl. fascism, techno-feudalism, etc.) – rather than a solution for addressing them?
  • How does actorhood (or the lack of) affect the relationship between privileged and marginal communities?
  • Can living (forests, rivers, soils) and non-living (algorithms, technologies) entities be attributed actorhood and be held accountable? How does it differ from 'human' organizing?
  • How can alternative ontologies help inform this analysis?
  • How can a gradual understanding of organization help us to understand variations in the degree of organizational actorhood and responsibility attributions in the relations between businesses and society?
  • What are the parameters of organizationality required for a responsible collective actorhood?
  • How can alternative ontologies, cosmovisions, and organizing experiences inform this critical reflection?
  • How to better account for situations in which marginalized actors are forced into fluid and precarious ways of organizing and/or have no choice to lessen the degree of organizationality to cope or survive?

item.title: Corporate Social Responsibility in Times of Societal Polarization, Politicization, and Securitization
item.content:encoded:
Dorothee Maria Winkler, Bern University of Applied Sciences

David Risi, Bern University of Applied Sciences

Christopher Wickert, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

Onna Malou van den Broek, Copenhagen Business School

Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has a long and influential history as one of the dominant paradigms in managing the business-society interface. For years, CSR has served as the normative and strategic blueprint for companies in managing growing societal expectations such as climate change, corruption, and inequality, fundamentally shaping corporate behavior across sustainability, ethics, and stakeholder engagement. Over the past decade, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria seemed to be moving from the periphery to the center of attention for companies, and the formalization and legalization of CSR-related criteria have reinforced the importance of corporate responsibility and consolidated its position as a central area of concern for business firms.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • What responsibilities do firms assume when navigating heightened political and societal tensions?
  • What does "responsible" corporate behavior mean in today's polarized global political economy?
  • How is CSR evolving to address the complex moral and strategic challenges of an increasingly divided world?
  • Do corporations counter populist and illiberal politics, or primarily align with dominant power structures?
  • How do firms recalibrate ESG and CSR commitments while maintaining legitimacy across diverse stakeholders?
  • Which role does CSR play in specific industries such as defense industrial complex, including defense-focused tech firms?
  • To what extent has CSR enabled corporate political activity (CPA) that influences democratic governance in ways that advance corporate interests?
  • How do new forms of "reverse CSR" or politically adaptive responsibility emerge?
  • How does the geographical context influence the conceptualization of CSR?
  • Is CSR diffusing from autocratic to democratic contexts as a tool of political signaling rather than social progress?
  • How do the underlying philosophical and epistemological assumptions of CSR differ across contexts?
  • How can established theoretical perspectives account for geopolitically fragmented CSR models?
  • How can nationalistic or "Western populist" CSR be conceptualized in a priori democratic contexts?
  • What theoretical frameworks need to be developed to account for the instrumentalization of CSR for national and geopolitical purposes?
  • Which role does CSR play in contexts of violent conflict?
  • How do security demands shape CSR's definition and scope?
  • What new priorities emerge when CSR is applied in the defense industry, particularly regarding process vs. product dimensions?
  • How do polarization, politicization, and securitization collectively shape CSR trajectories, and what role do businesses, governments, and other stakeholders play?
  • How do businesses weigh and prioritize imperatives posed by polarization, politicization, and securitization, and how does this influence their CSR agendas?
  • How do businesses recalibrate their CSR strategies to account for new and competing societal priorities?
  • How do governments integrate these dynamics when devising or revising CSR regulations?
  • Do we see emerging surveillance states arising from mutually beneficial collaborations between the defense-industrial complex (including tech firms) and governments?
  • Do we observe any sidelining or dismantling of international institutions and cooperation structures established after the Second World War?
  • How do societal stakeholders navigate this nexus when formulating expectations towards businesses and exerting pressure?

  • October 5, 2026: Online pre-submission workshop (participation optional)
  • August 1, 2027: Submission window opens
  • August 31, 2027: Submission window closes

item.title: Multinational Enterprises and the Sustainable Development Goals: Evolving Roles, Challenges, and Opportunities Beyond 2030
item.content:encoded:
Huda Khan, University of Aberdeen

Hussain Rammal, Adelaide University

Pervez Ghauri, University of Birmingham

Zaheer Khan, University of Aberdeen

Martin Meyer, University of Vaasa

The United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), adopted in 2015, provide a comprehensive global agenda addressing critical social, economic, and environmental challenges, with the target of achieving these goals by 2030. These 17 interconnected goals range from eradicating poverty and ensuring quality education to combating climate change and fostering sustainable economic growth. As the global community works toward this ambitious target, the role of Multinational Enterprises (MNEs) has become increasingly vital. MNEs, with their significant financial resources, innovation capabilities, and extensive global reach, are uniquely positioned to contribute meaningfully to the realization of these global objectives. However, integrating the SDGs into business strategies presents considerable challenges, especially in light of evolving institutional, political, and social dynamics.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • MNEs' Evolving Role in the SDGs' Agenda: Achievements, Gaps, and Future Directions - How can MNEs evaluate their contributions to the SDGs and adjust their strategies to meet the 2030 targets? What opportunities and challenges will MNEs face post-2030 in continuing to support the SDGs' agenda? How can MNEs address the lagging targets of the SDGs in their operations?
  • Managing ESG Backlash and its impact on MNEs' SDGs' Alignment - How does the ESG backlash impact MNEs' strategies for achieving the SDGs? In what ways do political and institutional pressures shape MNEs' SDG agendas? How can MNEs maintain their commitment to the SDGs amidst the growing scepticism toward ESG?
  • Institutional Dynamics and MNEs' SDGs' Engagement - How do formal and informal institutional logics influence MNEs' strategies for addressing SDGs in different host countries? How do institutional voids in emerging markets shape MNEs' SDG engagement? What roles do institutional actors (governments, NGOs, civil society) play in shaping MNEs' SDG commitments?
  • Business and Society Perspectives on MNEs and SDGs: Bridging IB and B&S Literature - How can IB literature inform B&S's understandings of MNEs' contributions to SDGs? How do MNEs reconcile profit motives with societal goals in their SDGs' strategies? What are the synergies between business model innovation and sustainable development in the context of the SDGs?
  • Leveraging Global Value Chains for Sustainable Development - What practical strategies can MNEs adopt to integrate sustainability into their global value chains to meet SDGs' targets? What are the opportunities for MNEs to collaborate with supply chain partners on SDGs' initiatives? How can knowledge transfer across value chains improve SDGs' outcomes?
  • Organizational Forms and Alliance for SDGs: Bridging IB and BAS Perspectives - How can MNEs and their partners in cross-sector alliances navigate the challenges of aligning values, beliefs, and power dynamics in SDG-driven initiatives? In what ways can partnerships between MNEs, governments, NGOs, and CSOs enhance the achievement of SDGs, particularly in areas such as inclusive development and climate action? What role do MNE headquarters play in supporting subsidiaries and local network partners to integrate global sustainability principles into their operations? How can MNEs collaborate with SMEs to achieve SDGs, and what benefits does this collaboration bring to local communities? How do strategic alliances contribute to the long-term sustainability of SDG initiatives, and what organizational forms are most effective in fostering these collaborations?
  • Micro-foundations of MNEs' Engagement with SDGs: Motivations, Leadership, and Human Capital - How do the personal experiences and values of top management, including the CEO, influence MNEs' strategies for addressing the SDGs? What role does diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) play in shaping top management's engagement with sustainability goals and advancing SDGs? How do leadership styles and top management teams influence employee engagement with SDG initiatives within MNEs? What mechanisms within MNEs' governance structures support or hinder the integration of SDGs into business models, particularly in the areas of poverty eradication, climate action, and social equity? How do individual decision-makers contribute to business model innovations that advance SDGs, and how do these innovations affect the company's long-term sustainability efforts?

  • October 30, 2026: Submission window closes

item.title: Our Oceans as a Business-Society Nexus: Advancing the Interplay of Blue Economy, Blue Governance and Blue Justice
item.content:encoded:
Matevž Rašković, Auckland University of Technology

Noemi Sinkovics, Newcastle University

Michelle Voyer, University of Wollongong

Nives Dolšak, University of Washington

Gurmeet Singh, University of the South Pacific

Our oceans make up 70% of our planet, provide transportation for 80% of global goods in volume and ensure the livelihood of over 3 billion people, including many of the global poor. Oceans represent the largest environment-humanity nexus on Earth in environmental, economic, geopolitical and global security, and socio-cultural terms. Yet, as planetary spaces, our oceans are often thought of as separate from humans in a human-nature duality, which limits research on the place-space embeddedness of business in particular environmental materialities like our oceans.

Appel publié par Business & Society. Lire l'appel complet sur le site de l'éditeur. Fiche de l'appel sur kerostig.

Potential topics

  • Business models, value creation, and distribution: How do different ocean-based business models create value, who captures the value and who bears costs across communities, ecosystems, and value/supply chains? What trade-offs and paradoxes emerge between economic growth and social/environmental objectives, and how are they justified, negotiated, or contested by various stakeholders and at different levels? How do firms build, maintain, or lose social licence to operate in ocean- and coast-related activities, and what triggers shifts in legitimacy?
  • Governance, accountability, and power across levels: How do governance arrangements (e.g., local, national, regional, transnational) shape who gets access, who is included/excluded, and how rules are enforced in ocean and coastal settings? When and why do 'good governance' arrangements still produce undesired social outcomes (e.g., exclusion, livelihood disruption), and what mechanisms explain this? How do firms, states, NGOs, and community actors coordinate or compete to frame problems, set standards, and allocate responsibilities and resources?
  • Justice, equity, and lived impacts: How are distributive, procedural, recognitional, and restorative justice concerns expressed in ocean and coastal contexts, and how do they translate into organisational and policy decisions? What forms of inequity arise in practice (e.g., displacement, access restrictions, benefit-sharing), and what interventions have been effective (or ineffective) in redressing them? How do gender, indigeneity, and marginalisation shape participation in governance and benefit-sharing, and what organisational and policy practices enable or constrain inclusion?
  • Ownership, stewardship, and legitimacy: Under what conditions are oceans treated as shared spaces versus commodified resources, and how do firms and states influence these framings? What governance designs or institutional arrangements support credible stewardship (beyond compliance), and how are these maintained or evolve over time? How do alternative understandings of stewardship and collective rights (including Indigenous governance) reshape corporate strategy, accountability, and legitimacy?
  • Risk, contestation, and the 'dark side': How do illegal, informal, or harmful practices (e.g., illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing, labour abuses, illicit trade) become embedded in ocean-related industries, and what enables accountability or impunity? How do firms manage reputational, legal, and operational risks linked to ocean-related activities, and when do risk-management approaches conflict with justice and sustainability aims?
